extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, examiners, academics, and policymakers concerned with §101 eligibility (algorithms/AI-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal-analytical criteria for determining patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, with emphasis on mathematical algorithms, abstract ideas, laws of nature, models/tools, and AI-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Criteria for Subject Matter Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must (1) be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and (2) qualify as patent-eligible subject matter by not being directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106.03 (statutory categories) and MPEP §2106.04/.05 (judicial exceptions and Eligibility Step 2B). The two-step/criteria approach is foundational to §101 analyses; both prongs must be satisfied for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Category Requirement (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must fall into one of Congress's four categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2106.03 provides detailed information. The categories distinguish 'things' (machine, manufacture, composition) from 'actions' (process). A claim not falling into one of these is ineligible regardless of other considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Exceptions: Abstract Ideas, Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have held that abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature) are exceptions to patentable subject matter under §101 and are not patentable per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Alice, Myriad, Benson, Flook, Diehr, Funk Bros., Chakrabarty. MPEP §2106.04 discusses these judicial exceptions and their scope; identifying whether a claim is 'directed to' one of these exceptions is the first part of the eligibility inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 PEG Definition of 'Mathematical Concepts'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG) defines 'mathematical concepts' as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition when evaluating whether claim limitations recite an abstract idea under the 'mathematical concept' subclass of abstract ideas. The PEG and its incorporation into MPEP §2106.04(a) are authoritative examiner guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly More / Eligibility Step 2B (Inventive Concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the claim must be considered as a whole to determine whether it contains additional limitations that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception (an 'inventive concept') to render it patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106.05 and Alice. 'Significantly more' is a relative notion and has been the focus of much case law; courts look for limitations that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application rather than a claim that pre-empts the underlying idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Application / Useful, Concrete, and Tangible Result (Diehr Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical formula or other abstract idea, when reduced to a practical application that produces a 'useful, concrete and tangible result', can render a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr distinguished claims that merely claim a formula from those that apply it in a specific, practical way. Cases like State Street and Arrhythmia show that transforming data through a machine to produce a practical result can support eligibility. Evaluate whether the claimed application meaningfully limits the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption Concern and 'Storehouse of Knowledge' Rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have expressed concern that patents which preempt the use of fundamental tools of science and technology (the 'storehouse of knowledge') would improperly monopolize basic building blocks and are therefore disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include Funk Bros., Le Roy, and O'Reilly v. Morse. Examiners and courts often analyze whether a claim would preempt all practical uses of a principle. Note: the document criticizes overbroad preemption reasoning when applied to novel, nonobvious discoveries that were not previously in the storehouse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic Tools and Models Are Not Patentable Absent Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental tools, models, and mathematical techniques (e.g., Fourier transform, linear algebra, numerical methods, Newton’s laws) are considered part of the basic tools of science and are not patentable on their own; patentability requires an application beyond the tool/model itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP and case law treat such items as in the abstract; examples in the text include Fourier transform, finite difference/element methods, Richards' equation, Newton's second law, Hooke's law, etc. To be eligible, a claim must apply these tools in a particularized, inventive manner rather than claim the tool itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Algorithms as Abstract Ideas — Need Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical algorithms, being akin to laws of nature or abstract ideas, are not patentable when recited alone; to be patentable they must be tied to a concrete application or implementation that confers 'something more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Benson, Flook, Bilski, Gottschalk v. Benson, and related Federal Circuit decisions. The presence of routine or conventional steps implemented on a computer is typically insufficient; the claim must do more than recite an abstract algorithm and say 'apply it on a computer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation in a Machine or Programmed Device Can Support Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing calculations/algorithms in a machine (e.g., digital filters programmed into microcode) or transforming data by a device may weigh in favor of patent eligibility if the implementation produces a specific technological improvement or concrete result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Street, Alappat, and signal-processing examples indicate that the transformation of data by a machine to produce a concrete output (e.g., waveform smoothing, filter operation) can be evidence of practical application. However, the mere fact of implementation on generic computer hardware is not automatically 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced Disclosure Considerations for AI Inventions (Algorithms as Material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments exist for an enhanced disclosure standard for AI inventions, including disclosing algorithms, because algorithms are a key aspect of such inventions and AI concepts are often ill-defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly and policy literature (e.g., Ebrahim, Penn State Law Review; USPTO AI report) discuss whether algorithmic detail should be required in patent disclosures for AI-related claims. This is a procedural/quality consideration: better algorithm disclosure can affect enablement, written description (§112), and the practical assessment of what the claim actually covers for §101 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption vs. Inventive Concept Tension (Alice and Post-Alice Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, courts ask whether remaining claim limitations contain an 'inventive concept' instead of relying solely on preemption analysis; Alice emphasizes looking for 'something more' in the claim that transforms an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice reiterated the test focusing on inventive concept. While preemption remains a policy concern underlying §101 doctrine, the modern test operationalizes eligibility through the 'directed to' and 'significantly more' framework; practitioners should frame arguments in these terms.
